title: Baat Athanni Ki
author: Sudarshan
tagline: A servant borrows half a rupee to repay a friend, and a magistrate who takes a far larger bribe sends him to jail.

overview.intro: Sudarshan’s "Baat Athanni Ki" ("The Matter of Eight Annas") is a short, hard-hitting story about injustice dressed up as law. Rasila is a poor servant who borrows a little money from his friend Ramzan and, when an opportunity comes, quietly repays part of it. The eight annas he still owe become the excuse for a beating, a forced confession and a six-month sentence. Set against a magistrate who has himself accepted a much larger bribe, the story asks who the law actually protects.

learningOutcomes: Retell how a half-repaid debt of eight annas leads to Rasila’s arrest, confession and sentence.
Explain the irony of Sheikh Salimuddin passing judgment while accepting bribes himself.
Identify how Sudarshan uses contrast between the rich and the poor to build the story’s argument.
Comment on the roles of Ramzan and Jagat Singh as the two opposing forces in Rasila’s life.

learn.title: The world of the story: service, hunger and a small debt

blocks.text: The story opens inside a world of quiet desperation. Rasila works for Engineer Babu Jagat Singh and is paid very little, money he sends home to his own family. When his children fall ill and he needs help, he asks his employer for an advance and is refused. In such a situation a man does not weigh morality abstractly; he thinks of sick children and of a friend who is willing to lend. Ramzan, a poor watchman, becomes the one human kindness in Rasila’s life, and it is precisely this kindness that later entangles him.

Notice that Sudarshan does not present Rasila as a hardened thief. He is a man who borrows, repays what he can, and is left with a residue of eight annas. Every later event grows from that residue. The story is built to make the reader feel the enormous distance between the smallness of the sum and the severity of the punishment, and to ask why that distance is allowed to exist.

learn.title: What happens: from the sweets to the sentence

items: Rasila overhears Jagat Singh negotiating a bribe and mentions it to Ramzan, who tells him that even the District Magistrate, Sheikh Salimuddin, is corrupt.
Jagat Singh sends Rasila to buy sweets worth five rupees; Rasila spends four rupees eight annas and uses the remaining eight annas to clear part of his debt to Ramzan.
Jagat Singh notices the shortfall, beats Rasila and drags him to the police, even paying a constable to make him confess.
In court Rasila admits the theft and asks for mercy, but Sheikh Salimuddin sentences him to six months in prison.
The closing irony: the magistrate who sentences a man over eight annas has himself taken a far larger bribe.

blocks.text: The movement from the sweet-shop to the courtroom is deliberately swift, and that speed is part of the point. A poor man has no buffer against the world: one missing handful of sweets becomes an arrest, an arrest becomes a confession, and a confession becomes half a year of his life. The story slows down only at the judgment, so that the reader must sit with the injustice of it.

learn.title: The people who decide Rasila’s fate

items.meaning: The poor servant at the centre of the story: honest by instinct, cornered by poverty, and honest enough to confess.
A poor watchman and Rasila’s friend who lends him money and names the injustice plainly.
The engineer and employer who takes bribes himself, yet punishes Rasila for a far smaller shortfall.
The District Magistrate who sentences Rasila to six months while his own corruption goes unexamined.
The paid official who helps manufacture the confession — the law bent to serve an employer.

blocks.text: Every character in the story is placed on a ladder of power, and Sudarshan makes the reader climb it downwards. At the top sits the magistrate, who can end a man’s freedom with a word and is himself dishonest. Below him is Jagat Singh, corrupt but respectable enough to command the police. Below him are Ramzan and Rasila, who share what little they have. The story’s moral force comes from watching the ladder work exactly as it is built to work.

learn.title: Themes: justice, corruption and the price of poverty

blocks.caption: Contrast that drives the story’s argument
rows: Rasila keeps eight annas to repay a friend
Rasila confesses and asks for mercy
Ramzan lends from his own poverty
The constable is paid to secure a confession

blocks.text: The central theme is unequal justice: the law is presented not as a neutral instrument but as something that reaches downwards and never upwards. A second theme is corruption and hypocrisy, embodied by a magistrate who sits in judgment while taking bribes. A third is poverty itself, which turns a moral choice into a survival choice. Finally there is friendship and mutual aid, the only warmth in the story, and even that is punished.

learn.title: How Sudarshan writes: irony as the main tool

items.text: The title itself — "The Matter of Eight Annas".
items.note: Naming the story after such a tiny sum forces the reader to compare the size of the crime with the size of the punishment before the plot even begins.

items.text: Ramzan’s remark that the magistrate is even more corrupt than Jagat Singh.
items.note: Placed early, this line prepares the reader for the courtroom ending, so the judgment arrives as confirmation rather than surprise.

items.text: Rasila’s confession and plea for mercy.
items.note: His honesty about the theft makes the severity of the sentence feel even less like justice and more like the punishment of poverty.

blocks.text: Sudarshan’s method is restraint. He does not editorialise at length or hand the reader a speech; he simply places acts side by side and trusts the reader to feel the disproportion. That is why the story is memorable in so few pages. Its irony is structural rather than decorative, built into the sequence of events and into the character of the man who passes sentence.

Questions on this story usually take one of three forms: a short note on the central idea, a character sketch of Rasila or Ramzan, or a question on the story’s irony. Whichever form appears, the strongest answers are built on the contrast between the smallness of the sum and the greatness of the punishment. Quote the sequence of events accurately, keep the magistrate’s own corruption in view, and end by naming the theme the story is arguing for rather than merely retelling the plot.

items: Anchor every answer in the eight annas: the title is the story’s thesis in miniature.
Use the magistrate’s bribery to explain why the ending is ironic rather than merely sad.
Distinguish Rasila’s honesty (he confesses) from the constable’s paid confession — the law is manipulated, not followed.

figures.caption: Figure: The path from a small debt to a six-month sentence
figures.description: A left-to-right chain: children fall ill → advance refused → borrows from Ramzan → eight annas remain → sent to buy sweets → eight annas used to repay → shortfall discovered → beating → paid confession → six-month sentence. Beneath it, a parallel track showing Jagat Singh and Sheikh Salimuddin taking bribes with no consequences at all.

figures.caption: Figure: The ladder of power in the story
figures.description: A vertical ladder with four rungs. Top: Sheikh Salimuddin, magistrate, corrupt but untouchable. Second: Babu Jagat Singh, employer, corrupt and respectable. Third: Ramzan, poor watchman who lends money. Bottom: Rasila, servant, who is the only one held to account.

keyPoints: The title names the whole theme: eight annas, half a rupee, is the sum a man’s freedom is measured against.
Rasila borrows from Ramzan not to steal but to repay — the shortfall is a partial repayment, not a plunder.
Jagat Singh takes bribes himself, which is what makes his righteous fury over the sweets so hypocritical.
The constable is paid to secure a confession, showing the law bent to an employer’s will.
Sheikh Salimuddin’s corruption is signposted early by Ramzan, so the ending lands as irony, not shock.
Rasila’s honesty in court sharpens the injustice: he does not deny the theft, yet receives no mercy.
The story is social realism: it argues that the law protects the powerful and reaches down at the poor.
Sudarshan uses contrast and restraint rather than long speeches, letting placed events carry the moral force.
examFocus: Central-idea question: state that the story exposes unequal justice, then prove it with the eight-annas-versus-six-months contrast.
Character sketch of Rasila: poverty-driven but honest — he borrows to repay and confesses in court.
Irony question: the magistrate who sentences over eight annas has himself accepted a larger bribe.

vocabulary.meaning: Half a rupee — eight annas, a very small sum of money.
vocabulary.context: The story is named after this sum, which a man’s prison sentence turns on.

vocabulary.meaning: Service, especially domestic or household service under an employer.
vocabulary.context: Rasila is in the seva of Engineer Babu Jagat Singh for a very low wage.

vocabulary.meaning: A bribe — money taken illegally to influence a decision.
vocabulary.context: Both Jagat Singh and Sheikh Salimuddin accept rishwat, yet only Rasila is punished.

vocabulary.meaning: A lawsuit or legal case heard in court.
vocabulary.context: The muqadma against Rasila is decided by a magistrate who is himself corrupt.

vocabulary.meaning: A witness in a legal proceeding.
vocabulary.context: The paid constable functions as a manufactured gawah against Rasila.

vocabulary.meaning: An accusation or charge levelled against someone.
vocabulary.context: The ilzaam of theft is laid on Rasila over eight annas of shortfall.

vocabulary.meaning: Mercy, compassion or pity shown to someone.
vocabulary.context: Rasila begs for dayaar in court, but the magistrate shows none.
Rasila is fundamentally imaandaar: he admits the theft rather than denying it.

questions.prompt: Why does Rasila need money from his employer?
options: His children are ill and he has no money for their treatment
He wants to buy sweets for himself
He must pay a fine to the police
questions.answer: His children are ill and he has no money for their treatment
questions.explanation: Rasila asks Jagat Singh for an advance because his children are sick and he cannot afford treatment; the refusal is what pushes him to borrow from Ramzan.
questions.commonMistake: Do not say Rasila borrowed to spend on himself — the need is medical and his family’s.

questions.explanation: Ramzan, a poor watchman and Rasila’s friend, lends him the money, and Rasila repays most of it, leaving eight annas outstanding.
questions.commonMistake: The lender is a poor friend, not a moneylender or an official.

questions.prompt: How much did Rasila still owe Ramzan when the shortfall is discovered?
questions.explanation: Rasila had repaid most of the loan; eight annas — half a rupee — remained, and that exact residue becomes the shortfall he is punished for.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse the eight annas owed with the five rupees of sweets he was sent to buy.

questions.prompt: What does Rasila do with the eight annas left after buying the sweets?
options: He repays the last of his debt to Ramzan
He gives it to the constable
He buys food for his children
questions.answer: He repays the last of his debt to Ramzan
questions.explanation: Given the chance to clear his debt, Rasila uses the remaining eight annas to repay Ramzan — an honest act that his employer reads as theft.
questions.commonMistake: The eight annas are used to repay a debt, not stolen for personal gain.

questions.prompt: How does Jagat Singh react when he finds the sweets money short?
questions.answer: He beats Rasila, takes him to the police, and even pays a constable to make Rasila confess.
questions.explanation: Jagat Singh responds with violence and then with the machinery of the law: he has Rasila beaten, arrested, and secures a paid confession so that the case against Rasila is made to look complete.
questions.commonMistake: Do not stop at the beating — the paid confession is what turns anger into a conviction.

questions.prompt: What sentence does Sheikh Salimuddin pass on Rasila?
questions.explanation: Despite Rasila’s confession and plea for mercy, Sheikh Salimuddin sentences him to six months of imprisonment over the shortfall of eight annas.
questions.commonMistake: The sentence is a fixed six months — do not describe it as a fine or a warning.

questions.prompt: Explain the irony in Sheikh Salimuddin passing judgment in this case.
questions.answer: The irony is that Sheikh Salimuddin, a man who has himself taken a much larger bribe, sentences Rasila to six months for a tiny shortfall of eight annas. Ramzan has already told Rasila that the magistrate is corrupt, so the courtroom confirms what the story prepared us for: the law is used to punish a poor servant while the corruption of the powerful goes untouched.
questions.explanation: Strong answers hold two facts together — the magistrate’s own bribery and the pettiness of Rasila’s offence — and show that the judgment is not justice but the exercise of power downwards.
questions.commonMistake: Do not merely say "the judge was strict"; name the disproportion and the magistrate’s own corruption.

questions.prompt: What role does Ramzan play in the story?
questions.answer: Ramzan is Rasila’s poor friend who lends him money, befriends him, and names the injustice of a system where the powerful are corrupt yet untouchable.
questions.explanation: Ramzan supplies both practical help and moral clarity: he lends the money that entangles Rasila, and he articulates the story’s argument by pointing out that officials like the magistrate are corrupt but never punished.
questions.commonMistake: Ramzan is more than a lender — he is the voice that names the injustice.

questions.prompt: Trace how a small shortfall of eight annas leads to Rasila’s imprisonment, and what the outcome says about justice.
questions.answer: Jagat Singh sends Rasila to buy five rupees of sweets. Rasila spends four rupees eight annas and uses the remaining eight annas to repay part of his debt to Ramzan. When the shortfall is discovered, Jagat Singh beats him, has him arrested, and pays a constable to secure a confession. In court Rasila honestly admits the theft and begs for mercy, but Sheikh Salimuddin sentences him to six months. The outcome shows that justice in this world runs along the ladder of power: a poor man is imprisoned for eight annas while employers and magistrates who take far larger bribes remain untouched.
questions.explanation: The full sequence demonstrates the story’s argument. Annotate each step and close by naming the theme — unequal justice — so the answer interprets the plot rather than merely recounting it.
questions.commonMistake: Do not present the sentence as logical or deserved; the point is the disproportion between sum and punishment.

questions.prompt: Do you think Rasila was right to take the eight annas? Discuss with reference to the story’s context.
questions.answer: Rasila did not steal to enrich himself; he used the money to repay a friend who had helped him in a crisis, and he was honest enough to confess in court. Judged against the corruption of Jagat Singh and Sheikh Salimuddin, his act is minor and his motive understandable. The story invites us to weigh the act against the conditions that produced it — poverty, sick children, a refused advance — and to reserve our strongest judgement for a system that forgives the powerful and imprisons the desperate.
questions.explanation: This is a discussion question, so a strong answer takes a clear position and supports it with evidence: the motive (repayment, not gain), the confession (honesty), and the contrast with the unpunished bribery of his employer and the magistrate.
questions.commonMistake: Do not simply say "stealing is wrong" without weighing the context and the unequal treatment the story exposes.
